description: AstroNova AI is an innovation-driven team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Peshawar. We aim to combine artificial intelligence, satellite data, software engineering, and creative problem-solving to address real-world Earth and space challenges. We welcome passionate developers, AI enthusiasts, data scientists, designers, and space enthusiasts who believe in collaboration, exploration, and building solutions with meaningful impact.
summary:
How can researchers distinguish real changes in Earth's burning activity from changes caused by satellite technology?

PyroSync AI addresses this challenge by harmonizing historical MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations from NASA FIRMS into a more comparable historical record. Our FireBridge engine processes observations on a common spatial grid, evaluates statistical and machine learning calibration methods, and transforms the resulting data into an interactive burning activity calendar.

Across 104 retrospective evaluation weeks in Pakistan, our validation-selected nonlinear model reduced mean absolute disagreement with VIIRS by approximately 71%, compared with unadjusted MODIS.

The platform combines interactive geographical exploration, sensor comparison, seasonal analysis, historical discoveries, uncertainty reporting and reproducible scientific exports. Our dataset inventory includes 94 annual archives across Pakistan, Australia, Brazil and Canada.

PyroSync empowers researchers, environmental analysts, land-management researchers and educators to investigate historical burning patterns using more comparable, accessible and transparent satellite observations.
details: Project Overview PyroSync AI, developed by ASTRO NOVA AI, is an interactive Earth observation research platform that addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. The platform bridges differences between generations of satellite instruments, enabling users to investigate historical burning activity through a more comparable and scientifically transparent record. The Problem MODIS and VIIRS observe thermal anomalies using different spatial resolutions, detection algorithms and observation characteristics. MODIS has a nominal active-fire resolution of approximately 1 km, while the VIIRS product used in our project has a nominal resolution of 375 m. Directly combining these observations can introduce artificial discontinuities into historical records, making it difficult to distinguish environmental changes from changes in satellite measurement capabilities. Our Solution PyroSync AI introduces FireBridge, a cross-sensor harmonization engine that processes historical NASA FIRMS observations using a common 0.25° spatial grid and UTC dates. Instead of treating every hotspot detection as an individual fire, the system measures distinct detected grid-cell-days. It evaluates calibration models using overlapping MODIS and VIIRS observations. The harmonized historical calendar prioritizes observed VIIRS measurements and uses eligible calibrated MODIS estimates where VIIRS archives are unavailable. Missing data, measured values and estimated values remain explicitly distinguishable. Scientific Innovation and Validation We evaluated five calibration approaches against an unadjusted MODIS baseline: - Historical multiplicative calibration - Robust linear regression - Seasonal multipliers - Regularized nonlinear regression - Gradient-boosted decision stumps Models were fitted on earlier historical observations and selected using chronological validation data. Across 104 retrospective evaluation weeks in Pakistan during 2023–2024, mean absolute error decreased from 264.37 weekly grid-cell-days for raw MODIS to 99.23 for the historical multiplier and 77.00 for the validation-selected regularized nonlinear model. This represents a 70.87% reduction in average absolute disagreement with VIIRS for the selected weekly research model. The calendar uses the simpler multiplier, while advanced weekly models remain separately available in the Science Lab. Application Features 1. Earth Time Machine — Interactive geographical exploration of historical satellite observations. 2. Compare Sensors — Synchronized comparison of MODIS, VIIRS, calibrated estimates and harmonized records. 3. Burning Fingerprint — Interactive historical calendar, annual comparisons and seasonal visualizations. 4. Historical Discovery — Evidence-based historical findings, percentile comparisons and cross-country seasonal profiles. 5. FireBridge Science Lab — Calibration experiments, model comparisons, error metrics, residual analysis and uncertainty reporting. 6. Report Studio — Scientific reports, CSV and JSON exports, charts and source provenance. NASA Data and Resources Our project uses historical NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 and Suomi-NPP VIIRS Collection 2 active-fire observations. Our dataset inventory includes 94 annual archive files across Pakistan, Australia, Brazil and Canada, with explicitly documented gaps. We use NASA product documentation and scientific guidance to support appropriate data screening, processing and interpretation. Technologies Used - Python - NumPy - Pandas - HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript - Statistical regression and machine learning - Geospatial grid aggregation - Natural Earth geographical boundaries - GitHub and GitHub Pages Impact and Benefits PyroSync AI supports environmental researchers, Earth scientists, land-management researchers and educators who need accessible historical satellite analysis. By reducing cross-sensor measurement inconsistencies, the platform supports historical seasonal investigations, environmental research and scientific education in Pakistan and internationally. Its lightweight, web-based architecture and freely available NASA datasets provide a foundation for accessible and scalable research tools without requiring paid AI services at runtime. Scientific Transparency PyroSync does not interpret hotspot detections as individual fires or burned area. VIIRS serves as a comparison reference rather than ground truth. Unknown satellite observation coverage, incomplete archives, retrospective evaluation and unvalidated daily allocations are documented. All major findings are connected to their supporting data, methodology and limitations. Future Development Future work includes expanding historical coverage, independent model evaluation, equal-area spatial aggregation, observation-coverage corrections, additional satellite products and collaboration with environmental research institutions.
